operand.headline: War & Seats: "To Nashville With Love" Benches Removed by Metro, Again
operand.dek: What Metro Nashville's latest removal of beloved community-built benches reveals about the war over our common spaces.

tokens.c: The war over benches continues.
Recently, benches were removed from Church Street Park, a tiny public park contractually managed by the Nashville Downtown Partnership (NDP).
The benches, placed there in March just as the downtown branch reopened after 9 months of closure following an explosion in the adjoining parking garage,

q.web-mqtlqg70: After nine months of closure, Nashville's Main Library reopened Monday.

tokens.c: had not received any publicly noticed concerns from Metro Nashville or NDP.

But on Tuesday, June 16th, the organizers behind the community-built benches were told that a Hub Nashville request had been submitted and that the city would immediately comply with the removal of the benches if the builders did not.

And only last week, photos were taken of a Nashville Department of Transportation truck with a community painted bench sitting in its bed. With the Metro Nashville budget now approved (along with NDP's), it seems the political establishment's tolerance for the community's reclamation of its public spaces is waning.

The removal of the benches is the latest salvo in a cold war over who has power over public spaces: unelected bureaucrats beholden to elite interests, corporate institutions devoted to extracting wealth from tourists, or the community itself.

body.caption: A photoshopped image of Mayor Freddie O'Connell removing a bench from in front of the recently reopened downtown library that was posted on the Instagram account @musicshitty

tokens.c: When NDOT contacted the community bench builders about the three benches that would be removed from Church Street Park, they were provided with photos of two of the three benches scheduled for immediate removal. They did not provide photos of the third bench that was removed from Church Street Park, which is managed by NDP and its vendor, Block by Block (the other named defendant in Traveler's lawsuit over the garage fire).
The third bench, the one that was removed but whose photo wasn't included in the email from NDOT, was painted. It said: "Please Don't Blow Up Our Library Again."

body.description: A hand-painted pale green wooden bench on a downtown sidewalk. The backrest reads "PLEASE DON'T BLOW UP OUR LIBRARY AGAIN" in rough red brushstrokes, and a red-and-yellow flower is painted across the seat. Behind it are a planted median with red-stemmed shrubs and a city street; a "Copper Ranch" storefront, a parked bicycle, and a "6th Av N" street sign are visible in the background.

body.text: In This House, We Sit Down

tokens.c: Benches, a tremendously popular and non-partisan public resource, appear to be at the heart of an ongoing power struggle between the government of Metro Nashville, elite institutions like the Nashville Downtown Partnership (NDP), and collectivist programs, like the one led by transportation and pedestrian advocates working under the name "To Nashville With Love."
Last year, public benches were removed on Korean Veterans Boulevard (KVB) at the direction of District 19 Council Member Jacob Kupin.

q.web-mqtlzw0t: The Nashville Department of Transportation replaced several popular benches along Korean Veterans Boulevard with large concrete spheres in recent weeks, citing city beautification efforts.

tokens.c: As per the Nashville Scene, this was done through coordination with NDOT and the Nashville Downtown Partnership. In a recorded interview with this author, he acknowledged that on taking office, he first noticed unhoused people occupying the benches and worked with the Nashville Department of Transportation to have them removed.

Months later, after the removal of the original metro benches became a consistent source of public ire towards Mr. Kupin, he claimed to me that he could no longer recall if the Downtown Partnership was involved in their removal. Yard signs have been spread denouncing his involvement in the removal of the KVB benches.

Mr. Kupin's flip-flopping on the topic of public benches appears to have caused great consternation not just among the public but within the Metro government itself. When, after working for years (by his account) to remove the benches, he then asked that the Boulevard in his district be allowed to retain the public-made benches, now former NDOT Director Diana Alarcon had four words for Mr. Kupin:
"You are killing me!"

body.caption: A yard sign stating: "IN THIS HOUSE, WE BELIEVE: EAST BANK BLVS SHOULD ONLY HAVE 2 CAR LANES, JACOB KUPIN TOOK THE KVB BENCHES, TESLA TUNNELS ARE FUCKING DUMB, SURVEILLANCE IS BAD, NDP BLEW UP THE LIBRARY, ZONING KILLS DREAMS"

tokens.c: The Downtown Partnership's role in removing benches from public spaces remains unclear. But an entity increasingly invested in the strict control of benches is Metro Nashville's Department of Law. Multiple bench advocates assert that they've been advised that the Department of Law has issued a legal opinion that any benches with paint on them should be considered "art" and must therefore be reviewed and approved by the Metro Arts Commission.

The connection between "public art" and "benches" is something the Metro has previously been fast and loose with. When the benches on KVB were removed, their replacements, large concrete sphere balls, were, according to NDOT, a form of "public art." The balls were donated by NDP.

q.web-mqtmvtwu0: KVB is a cut-through — let's elevate places like Walk of Fame Park and downtown greenways where we can placemake proactively.

tokens.c: The Metro Arts Commission, responsible for the placement of all public art, was not contacted at any point about the balls' installation, a legal requirement if Metro is to accept a gift of "art." If the balls indeed are art, the acceptance without approval through the Metro Arts Commission could constitute a violation of Metro code.

body.text: The Art of Tactics And the Tactics of Art

tokens.c: Further complicating the purported opinion of Metro Legal that painted benches may constitute "art" and therefore require Metro approval is that no benches currently in place were installed through a fully approved process.
NDOT has a program to permit items in the right-of-way; it is called "Tactical Urbanism" (TU).

Community organizers associated with the bench-building have denounced the red tape Metro has introduced into its in-house version of tactical urbanism, an approach to enhancing urban spaces that is, by definition, supposed to have less red tape. That Metro even has a formal "tactical urbanism" program is, to many people familiar with the ideology behind this concept, a contradiction of terms.

tokens:
The word "tactical" in "tactical urbanism" inherently denotes the class warfare at the heart of municipal infrastructure designed for the benefit of the powerful at the neglect of the less powerful. The term comes from theorist Michel de Certeau, who defined a "tactic" as an art of the less powerful: the maneuver of people who have no place of their own and must act, as he put it, "in the space of the other.

Dr. Craig A. Hammond of Liverpool John Moores University (School of Education) wrote about the tactics of the powerless in a 2017 paper.As micro-political manoeuvres, adaptive tactics can generate conditions for democratic and empowering manoeuvres, which can flourish between the gaps of strategic and organisational contexts. Individual tacticians should therefore seek ways of utilising the cracks, fissures, and inconsistencies that open up amidst the governmental tendencies of regulation and control.

tokens.c: A city department running an official "tactical urbanism" program inverts the term at its root: NDOT owns the right-of-way, sets the permits, and is beholden to the legal opinions of a law department overseen by a political appointee.

When the first community benches were approved for placement, NDOT communicated that the builders could move forward with placing them in designated locations, if, and only if, they could demonstrate they had a certificate of insurance protecting Metro from liability in the event that anyone was harmed while placing a bench.
It was in that email chain, in March 2026, that NDOT revealed they had removed 17 community-built benches that had already been placed without permits.

Contemporary media coverage recorded the organizers' sense of shock and betrayal. NDOT had been secretly removing benches without discussing with the builders, people with whom they were in constant communication on both the bench-permitting process and Vision Zero, a "zero traffic fatalities" program that many of the bench-building organizers serve on the advisory committee for.

q.web-mqtqr2vs0: This is a disappointing betrayal of the trust we had been building with NDOT

tokens.c: Robin L. Owen, a co-founder of this site and a co-organizer of "To Nashville With Love," said to the Nashville Banner:

q.web-mqtqr2vs0: This is a disappointing betrayal of the trust we had been building with NDOT

body.text: This is a disappointing betrayal of the trust we had been building with NDOT...in a meeting on November 21, 2025, NDOT assured us that they would not remove our benches and wanted to work with us to meet our demands. We now believe that they had already begun removing benches at that time.

tokens.c: That week, Robin appeared on CityCast Nashville. Her interview, intended to be a positive human interest story, was recorded prior to the revelation that NDOT had been taking the benches. Before posting the episode, CityCast re-interviewed Robin, wherein she unpacked her deep frustration with what she felt was duplicity on the part of NDOT and Metro Nashville.

body.text: It is unclear why NDOT, which has demonstrated the capacity to remove benches through its salaried staff, cannot place community-built benches in the right-of-way itself, voiding the need for unpaid volunteers to purchase a certificate of insurance to place wooden benches on public property. But more to the point, it is not clear why Metro has spent so much time and political capital fighting with community members who are asking for basic infrastructure, when there are many better uses of NDOT's time and taxpayer money.

tokens.note: There has not been an answer provided for why this is the case.

tokens.c: In March, 17 benches that had been taken by NDOT were recovered from the NDOT facility, rescued before formal permission for their recovery was granted. Since then, there has been an uneasy peace. I wrote about it at the time in exaggerated bombast, treating it like a clandestine hostage rescue.

tokens.c: In a subsequent oral history recording of the event, the reality turned out to be not far from the cinematic version I described on Substack.
Among the people who "freed" the benches was Kelly Chieng, the editor of this article.

In the wake of the "rescue" of the 17 benches that had been absconded with, a truce of sorts was reached, which has kept all benches in place under certain conditions. Community benches would not be removed; the arrangement had them in place as long as the bench builders were responsive to requests to fix maintenance issues and graffiti.

What this looks like in practice is something of a Kafkaesque farce where government workers are placing work orders with volunteer citizens, requiring them to cover graffiti within short notice or the community-built infrastructure will be removed by NDOT.

Emails from NDOT show an occasional stream of maintenance issues, with the bench builders fulfilling work orders generated by Metro employees and community members fulfilling maintenance requests within a day or two (comparable to light speed in government work-order time).

One particular email exchange between an NDOT employee and another got heated, with NDOT demanding that benches with "The F word" graffiti on them be repainted within 48 hours or they would be removed. Rebuking the demand that unpaid volunteers drop everything to paint over graffiti, one organizer opined:

body.text: If I write the same messaging on broken bike lane delineators or other dilapidated pedestrian infrastructure, will the operations team respond to them more efficiently?

tokens.c: NDOT's vision, as per its website, is: "to create a safe, sustainable, and balanced transportation system that supports choice and offers opportunities for vibrant neighborhoods for present and future generations."

q.web-mqufgh6u: We exist to create a safe, sustainable, and balanced transportation system that supports choice and offers opportunities for vibrant neighborhoods for present and future generations.

tokens.c: It's hard to square that with what they prioritize spending taxpayer money on: removing public infrastructure that might offend well-connected people, be those municipal benches that the unhoused sometimes lie on because of the failures of Nashville's housing and homelessness system, or removing beloved community benches under the ostensible reason that someone has written something "offensive" on it.

Benches funded, built, and placed informally by volunteers are being vandalized, and public workers are submitting work orders to private citizens to fix them, giving them 48 hours to do so; otherwise, the public infrastructure that the city is unable to provide will be taken away. Citizens are not allowed to place benches themselves without insurance policies protecting the city, and the city refuses to place benches for them, yet it is still willing to remove them because of vulgar graffiti.

The whole arrangement reveals the absolute absurdity of common spaces in Nashville. And it could be entirely avoided if the city just replaced the benches it has taken away or never installed. To a person, not one of the organizers I've spoken with about the benches asserts that their wooden benches are meant to be permanent infrastructure. The point, they emphasize, is to demonstrate that it actually is not all that difficult to provide infrastructure, and the irony that taxpayer dollars are being spent to remove benches is lost on none of them.

It is difficult to imagine a piece of public infrastructure that could be more innocuous and more apolitical than a public bench. But the incursion of Metro's Department of Law into NDOT's tactical urbanism, a program that even in its best possible implementation would be considered an attempt to "astroturf" actual collective governance of our common spaces, shows that there may be nothing more political than the public asserting its right to rest.

After nine months of closure, Nashville’s Main Library reopened Monday.

The downtown library closed in June after a fire erupted in the adjoining parking garage. NPL had initially targeted an opening date one month later, but the closure was soon prolonged after improvements to the building’s fire safety systems were identified during cleanup.

web-mqtmvtwu0.title: Benches Removed Along Downtown Boulevard, Sparking Backlash
web-mqtmvtwu0.text:
The Nashville Department of Transportation replaced several popular benches along Korean Veterans Boulevard with large concrete spheres in recent weeks, citing city beautification efforts. Eight metal benches previously stood on the north side of the six-lane downtown street, which was taped off as an active work site as recently as Friday, Aug. 15. All have been removed at the direction of NDOT, following collaboration with the Nashville Downtown Partnership and downtown Councilmember Jacob Kupin. 

“Those benches are a vestige of what Korean Veterans Boulevard could have been and what we hope a future East Bank Boulevard will be,” Kupin tells the Scene. “Early in my term, I advocated for these benches to be moved where they would be more useful and used by everybody. KVB is a cut-through — let’s elevate places like Walk of Fame Park and downtown greenways where we can placemake proactively.”
“The department recently began working with the Nashville Downtown Partnership to add more concrete spheres to Korean Veterans Boulevard as part of a public art and beautification project,” Cortnye Stone, NDOT director of strategic communications, wrote in an Aug. 14 email shared with the Scene. “We’re developing a plan to add an artistic element to the spheres and hope to have more information on next steps soon. We’re committed to ensuring public spaces across the city are accessible, functional, clean, and beautiful.”

web-mqtqivbi0.title: Tactical urbanism program
web-mqtqivbi0.text: Tactical urbanism allows Nashvillians to install their own street projects to make Nashville’s roads safer and more accessible for everyone. Tactical urbanism is an action-oriented approach using temporary measures to quickly test solutions to roadway challenges in the public realm. They can be on public streets, road, alleys, sidewalks, or parking spaces.

web-mqtr36wg0.title: Who put benches at nashville bus stops and why did the city remove them
web-mqtr36wg0.text: Late last summer, the Nashville Department of Transportation removed the benches lining Korean Vets Boulevard … but Pastor Robin L. Owen just happened to have one in her car. Since then, she and a team of volunteers have built dozens of benches to place at bus stops across the city, part of a nationwide movement; locally, the project is called “To Nashville, With Love.” She joins host Marie Cecile Anderson to talk about why these community-built benches matter, and share her reaction to last week’s news that NDOT was removing their benches, too.
